props.title: Demons

sections.content: **Demons** (1964) stands as a pivotal achievement in British horror, directed by Peter Newbrook during the golden age of Hammer-style Gothic cinema. The film builds on the psychological horror foundations laid by The Innocents (1961) and Night of the Demon (1957), weaving supernatural elements with psychological tension. Its approach to demonic possession predates and likely influenced later classics like **The Exorcist** (1973), particularly in its focus on the psychological deterioration of its characters.

sections.content: British horror cinema of the 1960s marked a crucial transition from the monster-focused features of the 1950s to more psychologically complex supernatural narratives. **The Witches** (1966) and **Eye of the Devil** (1966) followed similar thematic threads, exploring occult forces within seemingly civilized British society. These films established a distinctly British approach to supernatural horror that influenced later works like Blood on Satan's Claw (1971).

The film's visual style draws heavily from the Italian Gothic horror tradition, particularly **Black Sunday** (1960) and **Castle of Blood** (1964), while maintaining distinctly British sensibilities in its restraint and psychological focus. The cinematography by Desmond Dickinson, who also shot **Horror of Dracula** (1958), creates a brooding atmosphere that would influence later supernatural films. SUBHEAD: Influence on Modern Horror

sections.content: The legacy of **Demons** (1964) can be traced through subsequent possession films, from **The Exorcist** (1973) to more recent works like **The Conjuring** (2013). Its emphasis on psychological horror over explicit supernatural displays influenced films like **Session 9** (2001) and **The Blackcoat's Daughter** (2015), which similarly blur the line between mental illness and demonic influence.
